case.case_title: Soloman Dias v. Secretary, Ministry of Defence and Others

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the travel pass system restricting movement to and from Vavuniya infringed the petitioner's fundamental right to freedom of movement under Article 14(1)(h) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the travel pass system constituted an arbitrary and unreasonable restriction on his fundamental right to freedom of movement guaranteed by Article 14(1)(h), as it hindered his travel to Vavuniya in connection with his human rights work.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the travel pass system was a lawful security measure and that the petitioner's rights under Article 14(1)(h) were not infringed, as the restrictions were minor and justified.
key_facts: Petitioner is an Attorney-at-Law working on human rights and legal aid in Vavuniya.
On 05.09.2001, petitioner was allowed to travel to Vavuniya without a pass but was delayed and admonished on return for not having a pass.
On 04.10.2001, petitioner was required to obtain a six-day pass at the railway station before traveling to Vavuniya.
On 08.10.2001, petitioner returned by bus and was allowed to proceed without producing the pass.
The pass system was no longer in operation at the time of the decision.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court interpreted Article 14(1)(h) as guaranteeing freedom of movement but recognized that minor restrictions or formalities do not necessarily constitute infringements of this right if they are reasonable and not arbitrary.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the petitioner's first complaint was out of time and that the second complaint involved only minor irritations such as queueing and baggage checks, which did not amount to an infringement of the right to freedom of movement.
principles_established: Minor procedural requirements do not necessarily infringe freedom of movement.
Delays and formalities that do not prevent travel are not violations of Article 14(1)(h).
Timeliness of filing fundamental rights applications is essential.

outcome.holding: The court dismissed the application, holding that the petitioner's rights under Article 14(1)(h) were not infringed by the travel pass system.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(h) was central to the petitioner's claim that the travel pass system unlawfully restricted his freedom of movement. The court's reasoning and ultimate dismissal directly addressed whether the pass system infringed this constitutional right.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court held that the formalities of obtaining a pass and the minor delays experienced by the petitioner were no more than minor irritations and did not infringe his rights under Article 14(1)(h).
